note: Content source for the Product page, the landing page and front door. Audience is a product or executive reader, not a specialist. Keys beginning with an underscore are authoring notes and are never rendered.

hero.kicker: A weekly AI/ML brief that can prove it isn't making things up
hero.title: I stopped trying to keep up.
hero.titleAccent: So I built something that decides what's worth knowing.
hero.lede: One read a week, built around a single question: what would I regret not knowing? Seven items, each with the reason it matters and the evidence checked by code.

sections.title: Twenty minutes a day, and I was still behind

blocks.html: Every morning I opened five to ten tabs of AI/ML news and closed them twenty minutes later knowing roughly what I knew before. A model shipped. A benchmark moved two points. Somebody raised a round. Every item arrived with the same weight as every other item, and the work of deciding which ones mattered to my work fell entirely on me, at 7am, before coffee.

The twenty minutes were never the real cost. The real cost arrived weeks later, when something I had scrolled past turned out to be the thing that would have taken a project from idea to production in half the time. A missed capability is a missed quarter. The penalty for reading badly is not an awkward moment in a meeting, it is a slower time to value than the team next door.

Then the useful realization. I was trying to keep up, which meant trying to cover everything, and coverage was never available. Every approach I had was already a filter. The only open question was whether the filter was mine, deliberate and inspectable, or someone else's, implicit and tuned for engagement. So I gave up on coverage.

The target became the fewest items I would regret missing, and the system is allowed to say “quiet week, go build something”. Weekly rather than daily, because a daily brief optimises for missing nothing, and what that produces is a queue. Meaning needs a week of material before it exists at all.

sections._layout: Prose in the left column at about 58% width, the figure in the right at about 42%, top-aligned with the first paragraph rather than the heading. The heading and kicker span the full width above both. The figure is sticky while the prose scrolls past it, and under about 900px it drops beneath the prose at full width with sticky off. It carries the argument visually, so it must not be shrunk to a thumbnail.

figure._technique: Icons follow the slide-pitch-deck method: an inline <symbol> sprite referenced with <use>, one unique icon per row, each in a disc tinted to about 12% of its own colour. No icon fonts, no external assets. Palette is the page's, not the deck skill's.

sections._layout: One composed block, not two. The glass stat tile occupies the left column at roughly 45% width; the heading and prose fill the right, which is dead space today. No kicker: the heading carries the section on its own. Under about 900px the tile stacks above the prose and both go full width. The tile owns the numbers and the prose owns the meaning, so the prose deliberately does not restate 23% or 2x.
sections.title: The haystack compounds. The needle does not.

source.label: arXiv submissions, 12 months to Jul 2026 vs the year before

stats.label: more hours in your week to read it
the volume by 2032, if the pace holds

source.label: doubling every 6.0 years, computed from the same data

stats.label: items in one edition of this brief

sections.statsNote: Read left to right, that is the whole argument. The volume compounds, your week does not, and the gap between them doubles inside six years. The first three come from arXiv's own submission record, recomputed rather than quoted from one month. The fourth is the size of a real edition. Nothing on this page is an illustrative figure. A system whose entire claim is that it does not invent numbers cannot open with invented ones.

blocks.html: Those first three figures are measured, not sampled. They compare the twelve months to July 2026 against the twelve before, from arXiv's own submission record. Ten years ago the same source carried a third of today's output, and AI is the fastest-growing part of it.

Your reading week has not grown, and it will not. So the ratio of what exists to what you can personally examine gets worse every year, automatically, whether or not you get better at reading. Finding the one thing that matters is a search problem whose odds decline on a schedule.

All of that is before a single product launch, benchmark result, funding round or policy move. Research is only the part with a public counter on it. An edition of this brief carries seven items: a decision about the week rather than a summary of it, with the reasoning attached and the sources checked by code.

sections.title: The obvious fixes each fail in their own way

blocks.title: Curated newsletters
blocks.body: Written for a general audience, so relevance is a coincidence. They also need something exciting every single day, which is the pressure that manufactures noise.

blocks.title: Aggregators and feeds
blocks.body: Solved distribution, not judgement. I still had to read everything to find the two things that mattered.

blocks.title: Asking a chatbot
blocks.body: Fast, fluent, and no way to know when it was wrong. A summary you cannot verify is worse than none, because it feels like knowledge.

blocks.title: Save it for later
blocks.body: Later never came. The reading list became its own source of guilt rather than a solution to any.

sections.close: What they all miss is the same thing. None of them shortened the distance between a new idea and something running in production. They managed my awareness. The reason to read at all is to put a capability to work before it is common, and every one of these left that step entirely to me.
sections._close: Rendered as a single full-width line beneath the card grid, set apart by a hairline rule above it. It is the theme the four cards share, so it must not look like a fifth card.

sections._layout: Mirrors the numbered-steps pattern at trajectory.ai: kicker, one H2, then three numbered steps stacked down the left, each a short bold label plus two or three sentences. A single visual panel sits to the right and changes with the active step. On narrow screens the visual drops under its own step. Numerals are large, set in the display face, and use --faint so they read as structure rather than content.
sections.title: Three moves, in order, each one holding the next up
sections.lede: Everything reachable is narrowed to seven items, every line in them is traceable to a real source, and the thing doing the checking is graded too.

steps.title: Narrow hard, then explain the choice
steps.body: Everything reachable gets cut down to a handful of items. Each one carries the single reason it matters and the tradeoff it implies, plus the thread connecting the week, which is usually the part worth knowing. Once a week it goes further and turns one item into a 60-minute exercise grounded in my own repositories, so reading becomes doing.
steps.figureSpec: A funnel in three bands, widest at the top. Top band labelled EVERYTHING REACHABLE, middle band noticeably narrower labelled WORTH A LOOK, bottom band a small block labelled SEVEN ITEMS. Under the bottom band, one further tag reading ONE EXERCISE. Only the final count is measured; label the upper bands as design targets so the figure does not overclaim.

steps.title: Never let the writer mark its own work
steps.body: A summariser that occasionally invents a figure is not mildly flawed, it makes you confidently wrong in public. So three layers check the output, each catching something the one before it cannot. A model writes. A second model audits. Code proves the quoted evidence exists in the source, character for character.
steps.figureSpec: Three horizontal lanes labelled WRITES, AUDITS, PROVES. The first two lanes are drawn as model steps in the accent colour, the third in a plainer weight to signal that it is code rather than judgement. A short caption underneath: a model can invent a quote, a substring check cannot be talked into agreeing.

steps.title: Grade the grader
steps.body: The auditor is a model, so it gets its own graded test set: real output frozen with hand-written labels, re-run on every change. Its first version passed a brief that had been deliberately seeded with a fake valuation, a fake date and a fake investor, because a scoping bug meant it had never read the writing it was auditing. A test that has never failed is not evidence of anything.
steps.figureSpec: Two cases side by side feeding one gate. Left case labelled CLEAN DAY with a tick. Right case labelled PLANTED FAULT with a warning mark. Both arrows meet at a single box labelled GATE, with a short note that the suite only means something when one case is built to fail.

proof.label: false flags on a real edition, after one fix
proof.note: Measured across five runs before and after, not estimated. The other half of that result is still open and is named on the Roadmap rather than hidden here.

footer.note: Built in timeboxed sessions, planned and committed one phase at a time.

header._contract: THE HEADER IS IDENTICAL ON ALL FIVE PAGES. wordmark + wordmarkAccent render as one lockup in the serif face, the accent character in --accent. It is the site name and never changes per page. The page you are on is shown ONLY by nav.current. There is no descriptor pill, no page title, and no second active state in the header.
